To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
codon pair de-optimisation of RNA virus genomes is an artefact that is primarily mediated through increased CpG/Up A dinucleotide frequencies.
the attenuation of RNA viruses through codon pair de-optimization is an artefact due to the increase in CpG/UPA dinucleotide frequency, and that translation efficiency is not a factor.
codon pair usage is not an intrinsic property of viruses that attenuates replication but rather a proxy for the presence of CpG/UpAs in the genome that are recognised by innate immune sensors.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the mechanism by which viruses with high CpG/Upa dinucleotide frequencies are attenuated is not through the virus being intrinsically replication defective but through the innate immune response to these viruses.

codon optimisation and deoptimisation are not a good way to make attenuated viruses, and the reason for this is that they are not really changing the virus, but rather they are changing the host response.

the use of CP deoptimisation to reduce the fitness of RNA viruses is not a viable method for the generation of attenuated virus vaccines as it results in the unintended attenuation of virus replication through the accumulation of CpG and Up A dinucleotide motifs in the virus genome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
codon pair de-optimisation is a flawed strategy for the development of safe, attenuated vaccines.
codon usage and dinucleotide usage are not the same thing, and that the latter is a much more important determinant of viral attenuation than the former.
the use of codon optimisation/deoptimisation as a method to attenuate virus replication is an artefact.
